assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-firm trade models changed how the field understands selection, reallocation and the gains from trade. They shaped a large body of theory and empirical work, and they link micro-level productivity differences to welfare and policy. Within trade, the contribution extends well beyond the earlier new-trade-theory prize.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central model. Helpman's work, including Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, was a major parallel and extending contribution. Redding is a strong contributor to quantitative trade and geography but is more clearly a successor. Eaton-Kortum and Bernard-Jensen-style contributions sit outside this ballot item, so the credit is somewhat fragmented.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation, with firm-level evidence across many countries and wide textbook adoption. The timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would require Eaton-Kortum or empirical exporter-premium pioneers (Bernard, Jensen) to be credited alongside.
Helpman may be seen as better matched to a broader trade lifetime-achievement framing, which would change the laureate set.
I am relying on my own recollection of the literature, not independently verified sources.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural demand estimation for differentiated products (BLP) and dynamic industry models are the workhorse tools of modern empirical industrial organisation, merger analysis and antitrust. Their influence extends to trade, health and environmental economics.
assessment.attribution: The BLP demand framework is clearly credited to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Pakes also made foundational contributions to dynamic oligopoly (Ericson-Pakes) and to production-function and dynamic estimation (Olley-Pakes). Bresnahan, Reiss and Benkard have real but more specific claims, and the group can be drawn in different ways.
assessment.maturity: BLP dates from 1995 and is thoroughly validated by three decades of use in practice and policy. Timing is mature.
uncertainties: A three-person limit may exclude Bresnahan, whose empirical IO contributions are also seminal.
The balance between methodological and substantive-discovery contributions is a judgment call.
Dynamic-model credit (Ericson-Pakes, Benkard) is partly outside the proposed set.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) turned the study of cross-country income gaps into a quantifiable account of input misallocation across firms. It supplied a disciplined link between micro data and aggregate TFP, which is a central question in growth and development. It has generated a large research programme and informed policy debate in China, India and elsewhere.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow are the clear authors of the benchmark measurement framework. Restuccia and Rogerson developed related ideas in parallel, but Rogerson is not credited on this ballot. Banerjee-Duflo and others contributed adjacent work. The attribution to the first two is fairly clean.
assessment.maturity: The core paper is about seventeen years old, with extensive replication and extension. The framework has also faced critiques (measurement error, markups, adjustment costs), which are being absorbed into the literature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees misallocation as a measurement approach as opposed to a settled discovery about causes of income differences.
The omission of Rogerson from the credited names makes the parallel-discovery question harder.
Sensitivity of measured misallocation to measurement error and markup assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Credit-constraint amplification (Kiyotaki-Moore) and the financial accelerator are core to the modern understanding of why financial frictions propagate and magnify macroeconomic fluctuations. They underpin work on the Great Recession and macroprudential policy. The models are among the foundations of quantitative macro-finance.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is the clearest contribution. The financial accelerator is associated with Bernanke-Gertler(-Gilchrist), and Bernanke is already a laureate for related banking-crisis work, which complicates the ranking. Gertler's later work with Kiyotaki and Karadi on intermediation also matters.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with nearly three decades of validation and a post-2008 resurgence in empirical and quantitative work.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize for Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig could lower the perceived novelty.
Gilchrist's and Bernanke's claims to the financial accelerator affect how the three names should be selected.
Competing frictions-based approaches (Holmstrom-Tirole, Brunnermeier-Sannikov) are outside this ballot item.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The China-shock literature gave credible, widely cited causal evidence on local labour-market adjustment to import competition. It has informed political-economy and policy debates about trade and displacement. The work is influential in its own right. The broader task-based view of technology and wage inequality adds to the case.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock results are credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The tasks framework (Autor-Levy-Murnane, Acemoglu-Autor) and the skill-bias literature involve people not on this ballot, notably Acemoglu, who was already recognised in 2024 for other work, and Katz. Credit therefore depends on how the contribution is framed.
assessment.maturity: Around thirteen years of follow-up. Some persistent-effects findings are well replicated, while the size and interpretation of the long-run effects are still debated.
uncertainties: Whether the contribution is judged mainly as empirical evidence on one episode or as a general discovery.
The ballot mixes the trade-shock work with the broader technology and tasks agenda, which leaves open who should be credited.
Ongoing debate about the long-run aggregate welfare effects.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Staggered nominal rigidities, interest-rate rules and the New Keynesian framework underlie how central banks conceptualise and conduct monetary policy. The influence on practice and on academic macro is very large.
assessment.attribution: This is highly diffuse. Taylor (staggered contracts, Taylor rule), Calvo (time-dependent pricing), Woodford (the integrated modern theory), and Gali, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum, Smets and others all made central contributions. Any three-person selection leaves out several with strong claims, which is a serious attribution problem under the three-laureate limit.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decades of use in policymaking. Its relevance has been challenged and refined after 2008 and again after the 2021-22 inflation episode.
uncertainties: Which three names best represent a collective literature.
Post-2008 and post-2021 critiques of the framework's performance.
The Calvo, Taylor and Woodford choice is a judgment call and not an unambiguous result.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data gave new, credible measurements of intergenerational mobility and of neighbourhood effects, which have influenced both academic work and policy discussion. The data-and-measurement innovation is significant. Chetty also has important contributions in public economics beyond mobility.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader, with Hendren and Friedman as close collaborators on key papers. Katz is credited on the ballot for the Moving to Opportunity work. Credit for the mobility measurement sits with a fairly large team, so the three-name selection involves judgment.
assessment.maturity: The core results are about a decade old. Replication on other countries' data is growing, but long-run validation, causal interpretation of place effects and policy transfer are still developing. I would regard it as somewhat early.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to wait for further confirmation of the causal neighbourhood-effect findings.
Overlap with Chetty's other work in B021 may produce a different framing of what is being rewarded.
Earlier social-mobility theory (e.g. Becker-Tomes, Solon) is outside the ballot item.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models bring household heterogeneity and the marginal propensity to consume into monetary and fiscal transmission. This is an influential shift in quantitative macro, and the work has been taken up by central banks.
assessment.attribution: Kaplan, Moll and Violante (2018) is the central paper. It builds on the Aiyagari, Bewley, Huggett and Krusell-Smith tradition, so the incremental credit is partly synthetic. Other contributors, such as Auclert, are not credited on this ballot.
assessment.maturity: The framework is still recent, about eight years old, and its empirical and policy track record is still being established. It is likely premature compared with the more established candidates.
uncertainties: Whether the contribution will prove durable and transformative relative to its predecessors.
Credit versus the foundational incomplete-markets literature and younger contributors such as Auclert.
I have a professional proximity to macro work in this area, but I treat that as a disclosed matter and do not adjudicate it.
